title: Insulating around structural posts and columns to remove cold bridges
subtitle: Treating the cold-bridge effect where a steel or concrete post passes through the insulation envelope
excerpt: A steel RSJ or concrete column that runs from outside to inside a building bypasses the entire insulation layer and creates a cold, damp surface on the interior face. Wrapping the column with insulation and checking for condensation risk removes the problem without structural intervention.
sourceNotes: BRE BR 497 thermal bridging: understanding and calculation; CIBSE Technical Memorandum TM54 on thermal performance; ISO 10211 on thermal bridges in building construction.

glossaryTerms.definition: A continuous path of heat loss along a line, such as a wall/floor junction or a continuous steel beam, as opposed to a point bridge at an isolated fixing.
The linear thermal transmittance of a junction or thermal bridge, measured in W/m·K. Lower is better.

content.text: A structural steel post or concrete column that passes through an external wall carries heat from inside to outside far faster than the surrounding insulation can stop. Steel has a thermal conductivity of roughly 50 W/m·K; mineral wool is around 0.035 W/m·K. The column bypasses the insulation by a factor of 1,400.

On the internal surface, the column surface temperature drops well below room air temperature in cold weather. When warm moist room air meets that cold surface, condensation forms, often leading to mould growth at the column base. Wrapping the column in insulation keeps its surface temperature above the dew point.
What you need to know first

Check whether the column carries load from above. A structural post cannot have its surface area reduced without engineer approval; insulation is added around the outside of the column, not replacing any material.

Check fire compartmentation. A structural steel post inside a fire-compartment wall may need intumescent protection. If the column already has intumescent paint, confirm with a fire engineer before covering it with insulation.

Measure the column cross-section and the available space for insulation. A steel RSJ in a 100 mm wall cavity needs at least 50 mm of insulation on each exposed face to produce a meaningful surface temperature improvement.
Clean the column surface and allow to dry. Any rust should be wire-brushed back and treated with a rust converter before insulation goes on.
Cut PIR board panels to wrap each face of the column. For a circular column, use a phenolic foam board (more flexible) or cut triangular wedges that approximate the curve and fill gaps with foam. The
at each column runs from floor to ceiling; cover the full height.

Bond the PIR panels to the column with low-expansion PU adhesive foam. On a steel column with intumescent paint, use a compatible adhesive rather than PU foam, check the paint manufacturer's guidance.
Tape all panel joints with aluminium tape to complete the airtight layer.
Board over the insulation with 9.5 mm plasterboard for a flush finish. In a utility area, the insulation can be left as the final finish.

A 150×150 mm steel hollow section post in an extension wall. Room temperature 20°C, external temperature 0°C. Uninsulated column surface temperature: approximately 5°C (dew point at 50% RH: 9°C, condensation certain). With 50 mm PIR on three exposed faces: column surface temperature rises to approximately 14 to 16°C, above the dew point, condensation eliminated.

rows.symptom: Condensation continues to appear at the base of the wrapped column
rows.cause: The insulation was not taken down to floor level; the uninsulated column base is still cold
rows.fix: Remove the skirting and extend the PIR wrap to the floor; seal the base with foam.

rows.symptom: Mould returning on the plasterboard face of the column after two winters
rows.cause: Insulation layer too thin; column surface still cold enough to lower plasterboard surface temperature below dew point
rows.fix: Check the insulation thickness; add another 25 mm layer if space allows.
